findings.title: An order could be marked PAID for any payment_id in the request body
findings.description: Carried from the baseline review, finding 1. createOrder trusted the body’s payment_id; fixed so payment-service must confirm the payment (completed, this buyer, full total, not used for another order).
findings.root_cause: The order path trusted a client-supplied payment reference.
findings.technical_impact: Order state could advance without a completed payment (C-47 Invariant #2).
findings.business_impact: Goods could be released unpaid; seller payouts recorded against nothing.
findings.recommendation: None — closed. P6 re-traces the order → payment flow end to end.
acceptance_criteria: P6 traces a Mode-2 purchase and finds the order PAID only after payment-service confirms it

findings.title: Dependencies with known advisories remain in four Express services, payment-service and two apps
findings.description: Carried from the baseline review, finding 2. Closed for 22 apps (Next 15.5.29) and 15 Fastify services (Nest 11 / Fastify 5). Still open on main: gateway · auth · wallet · realtime on Express 4 / Nest 10; payment-service’s @stellar/stellar-sdk major; zod 4. P0 confirms tec-nbf and tec-brookfield main still pin next 15.5.12 (their PRs #32 · #28 are open, not merged).

evidence.observation: tec-nbf and tec-brookfield: dependencies.next = 15.5.12 on origin/main

findings.root_cause: Upgrades were done in batches; the Express services and two late-joining apps were not in the batch.
findings.technical_impact: Known-vulnerable framework versions run in production.
findings.business_impact: Exposure to published exploits on public endpoints.
findings.recommendation: Merge NBF #32 and Brookfield #28; after 1 Dec, upgrade the four Express services and the stellar-sdk major.
acceptance_criteria: npm audit --omit=dev reports 0 critical / 0 high in every service and app (P3 records the run)

remediation.note: The two apps close with these merges; the four Express services and the stellar-sdk major are scheduled after 1 Dec (Actions minutes). | 14 Nov — all of it, locally. The four Express services move to Nest 11 (the versions the other 16 services run — one Nest major across the backend), throttler 6 for auth, and each service's OWN express dependency (types only) to ^5: the old express 4 copy was where body-parser's advisory lived. npm audit --omit=dev high: realtime 5→0, wallet 5→0, auth 5→0, gateway 3→0. Code changes: the gateway's 404 used expressApp.use('*'), which express 5 refuses at start — the gateway would not have booted; now use() with no path, pinned by a test (CI never boots the gateway). auth: parseExpiry typed for @nestjs/jwt 11 (value unchanged — the 16 Oct ten-minute-session fix intact; boot logs 86400 s / 604800 s). Each service was BUILT AND BOOTED, not only tested: realtime (health, socket.io handshake), wallet against a throwaway DB (every money route refuses without credentials), auth (guards, CORS, lifetimes), the gateway against an echo upstream — a payment body arrives byte-identical, paths rewrite, the query passes raw, 200 KB intact, forged alg:none token 401. payment-service: its two highs came from toml 3 under @stellar/stellar-sdk 13, used only by stellartoml/federation, which the service never imports; an npm override pins toml 5.0.1 — signing untouched, and checked with the REAL library (a payment transaction signs, verifies and round-trips). NBF and Brookfield are on next 15.5.29. LEFT, recorded for the next cycle (not caused by this change; the code is the same): (1) stellar-sdk 17 for the A2U path, only with a real Testnet A2U payment — its unit tests mock the library; (2) auth's ThrottlerModule is configured but no ThrottlerGuard is registered — 25 logins in a row, no 429; the gateway's in-memory limiter is what limits auth today (auth is private); (3) auth answers a refused CORS origin with 500, not 403 — refused, but with the wrong status.
remediation.verification: npm audit --omit=dev on main: 0 high / 0 critical in gateway, auth, wallet, realtime, payment; each boots on Railway after deploy

findings.title: Fastify internal-key guards tested the raw URL for /internal/
findings.description: Carried from the baseline review, finding 3. Fixed in all 16 copies; CI checks the copies are identical.
findings.root_cause: Path check before decoding.
findings.technical_impact: An internal route reachable as a user call inside the network.
findings.business_impact: Not reachable from outside (the gateway decodes and refuses).
findings.recommendation: None — closed.
acceptance_criteria: scripts/check-guard-copies.sh passes on main

findings.title: The Hub's Content-Security-Policy still allows 'unsafe-inline' and 'unsafe-eval' scripts
findings.description: Carried from the baseline review, finding 4. connect-src was narrowed to named hosts (tec-app #324, closed). script-src still carries 'unsafe-inline' 'unsafe-eval'; the Pi SDK load path has to change first. The header is public, so this is not withheld.
findings.root_cause: The Pi SDK bootstrap relies on inline script.
findings.technical_impact: An injected script would not be blocked by CSP.
findings.business_impact: CSP gives no second line of defence against XSS on the payment hub.
findings.recommendation: Move the Pi SDK bootstrap to a nonce- or hash-allowed script, then drop 'unsafe-inline' and 'unsafe-eval'.
acceptance_criteria: The Hub's production CSP header has no 'unsafe-inline' or 'unsafe-eval' in script-src
A Pi Browser sign-in and Mode-2 payment still work

remediation.note: 'unsafe-inline' is gone from the Hub's script-src: the middleware sends a fresh nonce per request with 'strict-dynamic' (src/lib/csp.ts, the one place the policy is written; next.config.js no longer carries it). The boot scripts, the Pi SDK <Script> and the sign-in landing page carry the nonce; object-src 'none' and base-uri 'self' added; violations go to /api/csp-report (logged without query strings or script samples — the landing page's address holds a one-time token). On a production build every page is dynamic and every executable script on seven pages carries the header's nonce; in Chromium the pages hydrate, the boot scripts run, and an injected onerror handler is refused (the old policy ran it). 'unsafe-eval' is still in the ENFORCED policy: the Pi SDK (sdk.minepi.com) could not be read from here, and if it calls eval, removing it breaks sign-in for everyone. A report-only twin refuses eval; the Hub's own build has no eval / new Function in any chunk. Left: a Pi Browser sign-in + Mode-2 payment on the deployed Hub; if they leave no 'eval' line in the csp.violation log, set CSP_ENFORCE_NO_EVAL=1 on Vercel and redeploy.
remediation.verification: Production Hub response: Content-Security-Policy script-src has a nonce and no 'unsafe-inline' (and, after the switch, no 'unsafe-eval'); a Pi Browser sign-in and Mode-2 payment work

findings.title: Template fixes do not reach the apps made from it — the mechanism is not on main yet
findings.description: Carried from the baseline review, finding 5. The template-sync mechanism (manifest, check/apply script, weekly fleet-drift job) is built in tec-template-base #56, but P0 finds no template-sync.json on origin/main: until it merges, nothing reports drift.
findings.root_cause: Apps are copies of the template with no link back.
findings.technical_impact: Fixes made once are missing from some apps for weeks.
findings.business_impact: Uneven security and sign-in behaviour across the 24 apps.
findings.recommendation: Merge tec-template-base #56 and the 20 app PRs that adopt it.
acceptance_criteria: template-sync.json exists on tec-template-base main
The first fleet-drift run lists no app as drifted, or opens one issue that names each

remediation.note: The mechanism exists; it is not on main yet. Run 6: template-sync is on the template branch; Life and Zone still miss 15–16 shared files (fleet screens, help, feedback, manifest, Pi Browser e2e). | 14 Nov: Life and Zone brought onto the template (apply + the three markers by hand: state screens, /help, the feedback card and its shared route, the manifest from lib/app-meta.ts, Open Graph, the Pi Browser e2e project, jsx-a11y, the example route). Two of Life's own rules met template files: its feedback test pinned the old variable name (the invariant — server label wins — still holds, now as APP_SOURCE, and the test also pins APP_SOURCE = 'life'); its no-raw-colour rule now exempts lib/app-meta.ts (a manifest cannot read a CSS variable) with a new test that pins that colour to the dark --tec-bg token. template-sync check: all 20 template apps match. What is left is the merge.
remediation.verification: fleet-drift's first run on main lists no app as drifted

Stopping a service pages within 5 minutes

findings.title: Hand-written input validation in seven services; low coverage floors; very long Hub files
findings.description: Carried from the baseline review, finding 7 (the Ecommerce dead middleware part is closed). P2 measures this.

evidence.observation: P2 measured: no schema validation library in analytics · commerce · identity · kyc · notification · realtime · storage

findings.root_cause: Services written before the shared validation pattern.
findings.technical_impact: Unvalidated edge cases reach the services.
findings.business_impact: Bugs cost more to find.
findings.recommendation: P2 lists the services and files; remediation adopts zod at each edge.
acceptance_criteria: Every service validates request bodies with a schema library
No Hub source file over 600 lines without a recorded reason

remediation.note: One way to read a request body: parseBody (tec-service-template/src/middleware/parse-body.ts) — the schema's output or a 400 naming each field, never its value; byte-identical in every service that carries it (scripts/check-guard-copies.sh). Applied at every body edge with a gap in kyc, storage, notification, realtime, identity and commerce, each with a test red on the old code. What it caught besides types: DELETE /notifications/device-tokens with no token unregistered EVERY device of the caller's (Prisma reads `token: undefined` as no condition); a storage purge given `keys` that was not a list answered 'deleted 0'; a watchlist `done: "true"` un-ticked the reminder; a review rating of 1000 was averaged into a product's stars; a gift's `days` could be NaN. Two security holes surfaced and are recorded separately (0046, 0047). Left as they were, on purpose, because they already check every field by hand with a named reason: analytics' intent observation (a pure, tested validator), identity's internal alert / deletion-ledger / erasure / users controllers, commerce's payout. Hub: no source file over 600 lines without a recorded reason — src/__tests__/file-size.test.ts lists the four that are, each with its reason and a ceiling it may not grow past (dictionaries and the domain registry are data, exempt).
remediation.verification: Each service's suite on main green, including its *-input.spec.ts; check-guard-copies.sh green in CI

findings.title: One HS256 JWT secret is shared by 20 services and 24 apps
findings.description: Carried from the baseline review, finding 8. A leak of the secret anywhere forges any identity everywhere. One Redis is the whole event bus (P9/P10 assess).
findings.root_cause: Symmetric signing chosen early; every verifier holds the signing key.
findings.technical_impact: The blast radius of one leaked variable is the whole platform.
findings.business_impact: Account takeover of any user, admin included, from one leak.
findings.recommendation: Finish the rotation plan: asymmetric signing (the issuer alone holds the private key).
acceptance_criteria: Only tec-auth-service holds a signing key
Every verifier holds only a public key

remediation.note: Last step of the rotation plan (asymmetric signing); backend, after 1 Dec.

findings.title: window.Pi.authenticate / createPayment are called directly, around the Pi Abstraction Layer
findings.description: PiRuntime (the PAL) exists in the template and the Hub and wraps authenticate/createPayment with the circuit breaker, but the sign-in (pi-auth.ts) and payment (pi-payment.ts) paths call window.Pi directly. 80 call sites across 25 repositories (3 per template app; Hub 4; Commerce 6). The inline Pi.init in layout.tsx is the accepted exception (it runs before any module loads).

evidence.observation: PiRuntime.authenticate checks piCircuitBreaker.canAttempt(); createPayment wraps pi.createPayment

findings.root_cause: The PAL was added after the payment and sign-in code and only pi-session.ts was moved onto it.
findings.technical_impact: A Pi SDK change needs 80 edits, not one (risk R1); the circuit breaker does not protect sign-in or payment.
findings.business_impact: A Pi SDK update can break payments platform-wide with no single fix point (C-12 risk R1, P0).
findings.recommendation: Route pi-auth.ts and pi-payment.ts through PiRuntime in the template, then let template-sync carry it to the apps.
acceptance_criteria: architecture_checks.py P1-C16 reports only layout.tsx init lines
Payment and sign-in tests mock PiRuntime, not window.Pi

remediation.note: Sign-in and payment call PiRuntime. pal-boundary.test.ts fails on any direct call (shown red on the old code). template-sync makes pi-auth.ts and the test shared and pi-payment.ts carry the marker, so an app that drifts back is reported weekly. Not yet done: the Hub, Commerce, Assets and Ecommerce (outside the template; their own PAL work, P10).
remediation.verification: architecture_checks.py P1-C16 on main lists only layout.tsx init lines for the template apps

findings.title: Marketplace listing prices in Pi are stored as Float
findings.description: tec-asset-service AssetListing.price is Float, read and written by the marketplace (listings, minPrice/maxPrice filters). C-47 §12 and C-71 require DECIMAL(20,8) for Pi amounts; a binary float cannot hold 0.1 π exactly.
findings.root_cause: The model predates the DECIMAL rule.
findings.technical_impact: Rounding errors in prices; a price charged may differ from the one listed in the last digits.
findings.business_impact: A buyer can be charged an amount that is not the listed one.
findings.recommendation: Migrate price to Decimal(20,8) (expand–contract, after a data check) and carry it as a string at the API edge.
acceptance_criteria: schema.prisma: price Decimal @db.Decimal(20, 8)
A migration ships it; a test lists 0.1 π and reads back exactly 0.10000000

remediation.note: Still open (re-measured in Run 6: asset price is Float at HEAD). P4 did not do the expand–contract migration; it needs a production row count first and changes the Assets contract (price as a string). The P4 report said 'fixed locally' in error — corrected.

findings.title: Three other money-like columns are Float
findings.description: wallet-service Account.balance (an unused model kept from the initial migration — the live Wallet.balance is Decimal(20,8)); analytics DailyMetric.total_volume (a projection, eventual by design); life-service LifeGoal.target_amount (a self-declared target). None moves money.

evidence.observation: balance Float — model commented as unused

findings.root_cause: Rule applied to the financial core first.
findings.technical_impact: Small rounding in displayed totals and targets.
findings.business_impact: None material.
findings.recommendation: Drop the unused Account model (owner decision); move the other two to Decimal when their tables are next migrated.
acceptance_criteria: architecture_checks.py P1-C06 reports no hit, or each remaining hit carries a recorded ACCEPTED_RISK

remediation.note: Needs a production row count of the wallet Account table before it is dropped; still open after P4.

findings.title: The internal-key check compares string length, not byte length, before timingSafeEqual
findings.description: In four places the guard checks internalKey.length === secret.length and then timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(...)). A header of the same character count but a different byte count (any non-ASCII character) makes timingSafeEqual throw, so the request ends as a 500 instead of a 401/403. It is not a bypass: a throw never authorises.

evidence.observation: length compared on strings, then timingSafeEqual on Buffers

findings.root_cause: Four hand-written copies instead of the shared guard.
findings.technical_impact: A malformed header produces a 500 and an error log.
findings.business_impact: Noise in error monitoring; a 5xx counted against the SLO.
findings.recommendation: Compare Buffer byte lengths (or use the shared validateInternalKey) in all four.
acceptance_criteria: A test sends a same-length non-ASCII key and gets 401/403, not 500, in each of the four

remediation.note: All 18 copies (the search found 5; the fix looked for the pattern, not the name) compare Buffer.byteLength. tec-auth-service internal-key-bytes.spec.ts is red on the old code and green now. tsc + jest green in auth, payment, gateway, wallet, analytics, connection.

findings.title: payment-service's rate limiter could key on a userId from the body or the query
findings.description: createRateLimiter built its key as ip + (req.userId ?? req.body.userId ?? req.query.userId). A key must come only from the verified identity (C-47 P6). Every limiter on payment.routes.ts runs after authenticate(), which always sets req.userId, so the fallback was dead code — not reachable. Fixed anyway: a dead fallback is a live one the day a route is ordered differently.

evidence.observation: userId from req.userId, else body, else query

findings.root_cause: A fallback written for routes without authentication.
findings.technical_impact: None reachable today.
findings.business_impact: None.
findings.recommendation: Key on req.userId only (done).
acceptance_criteria: A request with a different body userId lands in the same bucket (test in security.test.ts)

remediation.note: Reassessed: every payment rate limiter runs after authenticate(), so the fallback was not reachable. The key is now the verified identity only; a test pins that a body userId opens no fresh bucket (red on the old code). Published, since it was never exploitable.

findings.title: The baseline disagrees with itself on the type of a Pi amount in an API
findings.description: ADR-009 (C-64:238-256) makes a payment request's amount a number (z.coerce.number() at the BFF). C-71 §3 says a string in API responses. tec-core-backend CLAUDE.md:333 says 'string in all API contracts', which contradicts ADR-009 for requests. The one P1 hit (Hub POST /api/bff/wallet/withdraw, amount: z.string().regex(…)) is a wallet call, not a payment endpoint, and keeps precision — it is not counted as a violation, but the baseline cannot say whether it is right.

evidence.observation: amount → number; string FORBIDDEN on payment endpoints
DECIMAL(20,8) in DB · String in API responses
'string in API responses' and 'string in all API contracts'

findings.root_cause: Two rules written at different times for requests and responses, then generalised.
findings.technical_impact: Reviewers apply opposite rules to the same field.
findings.business_impact: Inconsistent contracts between apps and services (P5).
findings.recommendation: Owner decision: one sentence in C-71 covering requests and responses (e.g. number on payment requests per ADR-009, string elsewhere), then align the backend CLAUDE.md.
acceptance_criteria: C-71 and ADR-009 state one rule for request amounts
CLAUDE.md files quote it without contradiction

remediation.note: One rule: DECIMAL(20,8) in the database; a decimal string wherever an amount leaves a service; a number only in a payment request (ADR-009). The ADR stands because it ranks above the spec.

findings.title: The port authority C-20 does not describe eight of the deployed services
findings.description: P0 counts 20 deployable services plus backup-job in tec-core-backend (and the shared library and service template). C-20, the backend-services and port authority, names 12. tec-business, tec-life, tec-nexus, tec-platform, tec-search and tec-trust-service and tec-backup-job do not appear in it at all; tec-ai and tec-connection-service appear once each. Those services start with PORT required (no default in main.ts). C-02 §1 names their ports (:5012–:5019) in one line; the port authority does not. Gate B is met for them through their code, C-02 and their app charters.

evidence.observation: 23 entries: 20 services · backup-job · shared · template; 8 with port_required = true
business 0 · life 0 · nexus 0 · platform 0 · search 0 · trust 0 · backup 0 · ai 1 · connection 1

findings.root_cause: Services were added after C-20 was last rewritten; check-drift checks only the services C-20 lists.
findings.technical_impact: No canonical statement of what those services own, which port they use, or who calls them.
findings.business_impact: Ownership questions (C-68) for eight services are answered from memory.
findings.recommendation: Extend C-20 to every deployed service (role, owner, port source, network) and make check-drift compare the service list itself.
acceptance_criteria: Every directory in tec-core-backend with a package.json and a Dockerfile appears in C-20
check-drift.py fails when one does not

remediation.note: The auditor's error: the search looked for 'tec-<name>', and C-20's table names services by their short name ('life', 'ai' …). C-20 lists all 20 services with their ports. What was real: check-drift.py's service list is typed by hand, so a new service would be invisible to it — it now fails on any service in code it does not list (shown firing by removing 'trust' from the list).

findings.title: Production dependencies carry high advisories that a non-breaking update removes
findings.description: npm audit --omit=dev on every app lock file on main: 14–15 high per template app. The fixable-in-range ones are axios and follow-redirects (outbound requests: prototype-pollution gadget, credential headers across redirects), brace-expansion, nanoid, sharp, browserslist, fast-uri, socket.io-parser and source-map-js. @yasser172/tec-sdk is itself flagged because it pins a vulnerable axios, and it has not been published since 13 Sep, so every app inherits it. postcss and rollup need a major (next 16, @sentry/nextjs 11) and are build-time only.

evidence.observation: per-lock counts and the critical/high package list with fix availability

findings.root_cause: Lock files not refreshed since the advisories were published; the SDK pins its own axios.
findings.technical_impact: Server-side BFF calls go through a vulnerable HTTP client.
findings.business_impact: A crafted upstream response or redirect could leak a header or skew a request.
findings.recommendation: Publish TEC-SDK with a fixed axios; then npm audit fix (no --force) in the template and let template-sync carry the lock refresh; leave the majors for a planned upgrade.
acceptance_criteria: npm audit --omit=dev reports no high fixable without a major in any app lock on main

refs: 24 apps + the Hub (one commit each, 14 Nov)
remediation.note: npm update within the declared ranges (npm audit fix crashes on these trees: 'edgesOut'). No SDK release was needed: tec-sdk declares axios ^1.6.7, so the lock moves it. Apps: 14 high → 5 (Life 5 → 3). Hub: 17 high + 2 CRITICAL (protobufjs, websocket-driver) → 10 high, 0 critical. Every remaining high needs a major — @sentry/nextjs 11, next 16 (postcss, rollup), firebase 13 for the Hub (firestore → grpc-js, undici) — or is zod (0020). Only lockfiles changed; every suite green; production builds of the template, Commerce, Zone and the Hub pass.
remediation.verification: npm audit --omit=dev on main: no high or critical with a non-major fix, in any repo

findings.title: zod 3 has a high memory-exhaustion advisory with no fix short of zod 4
findings.description: Present in 38 lock files: every app, TEC-SDK, and 13 backend services (ai, business, connection, gateway, identity, life, nexus, payment, platform, search, template, trust, wallet). An oversized collection sent to a constrained schema can exhaust memory. Body-size limits bound it (Fastify 1 MB default; Vercel 4.5 MB); not measured per route here.

evidence.observation: zod high, fixAvailable: false, in 38 locks

findings.root_cause: zod 3 is past its fix line; zod 4 is a major.
findings.technical_impact: A request can cost a process more memory than it should.
findings.business_impact: Availability, not data.
findings.recommendation: Plan the zod 4 migration (already open under TEC-AUDIT-0002); until then keep explicit body-size limits on every route that validates arrays.
acceptance_criteria: No lock file on main resolves zod < 4
or every validated route has a stated body limit

refs: 23 apps + the Hub (one commit each, 14 Nov)
remediation.note: 14 Nov. zod 4 everywhere it is a direct dependency: the template and 23 apps (one change: z.record() takes its key schema, in payment/create), the Hub, 13 backend services (one change: payment-service's PI_SANDBOX messages move to zod 4's error hook, word for word), and TEC-SDK — prepared as 2.0.0, because it exports zod schemas. The packed 2.0.0 was installed temporarily in the template, Ecommerce and the Hub: type-check, every test and a production build pass, and zod 4 is the only zod in their tree; restored after. Found on the way: payment-service's env test built its own copy of the schema and never read env.ts; it now loads the real module (red on the old env.ts under zod 4). LEFT: until TEC-SDK 2.0.0 is published (its release workflow, after GitHub Actions is back) and every consumer moves to ^2.0.0, each app still resolves zod 3 INSIDE @yasser172/tec-sdk — isolated (apps import only TecSdk, never its schemas), but present in the lock, so the acceptance criterion is not yet met. Process notes, recorded so they are not repeated: (1) a loop ran template-sync apply over Commerce, Assets, Ecommerce and the Hub — apps not made from the template — copying ~45–100 template files into each; caught by their tests and the Hub's 109-file commit, undone file by file (every new file checked to be a template copy) before any push; apply now refuses an untracked repo (tec-template-base c851c65, with a test). (2) The disk filled mid-run; results printed then ("0 errors") were false — a corrupted node_modules was reinstalled and every number above was re-measured after space was freed.
remediation.verification: After the SDK release: npm ls zod on main shows only 4.x in every app; npm audit --omit=dev lists no zod

findings.title: The Hub keeps a stale second lock file that pins Next 15.5.12
findings.description: tec-frontend/package-lock.json (last changed in #120) locks next 15.5.12 with a critical advisory, while the workspace root lock — the one Vercel installs from — locks 15.5.29. Production runs 15.5.29: the build log of the live deployment says "Detected Next.js version: 15.5.29" [Runtime Verified]. The stale file misleads scanners and people.

findings.technical_impact: A false critical in every scan.
findings.business_impact: Noise hides the real ones.
findings.recommendation: Delete tec-frontend/package-lock.json.
acceptance_criteria: Only the root lock file exists on main

remediation.note: Stale lock deleted; CI cache keys hash the root lock. Proved in a clean worktree: install inside tec-frontend resolves Next 15.5.29 from the root lock and creates no new lock. committed locally — pushed when GitHub Actions is back

findings.description: The repository root declares Nest 10, bcrypt 5, axios and others, with build/start scripts for a dist/main that does not exist. Nothing installs it: no Dockerfile or workflow runs npm at the root, and scripts/ imports only Node built-ins. Its lock has critical proxy-addr and tar advisories. Not deployed, but a scanner and a reader both take it for the backend.

findings.title: The gateway's public-route list is wider than it needs to be
findings.description: Swagger UI (/api/docs) is served in production without a token and outside rate limiting. '/api/commerce/products' is a prefix exemption for every method, writes included; commerce-service verifies the token on its writes itself (product.controller.ts getUserId, HS256), so nothing is open today, but the gateway gives no second check. '/metrics' is listed public with no handler behind it.

evidence.observation: swagger-ui mounted; /api/docs excluded from the rate limiter

findings.root_cause: Exemptions written as prefixes for reads and never narrowed.
findings.technical_impact: Defence in depth is one layer thinner for product writes; the API surface is published.
findings.business_impact: Low.
findings.recommendation: Exempt products for GET only; serve /api/docs only outside production (or behind the internal key); drop '/metrics'.
acceptance_criteria: A POST to /api/commerce/products without a token is refused at the gateway
GET /api/docs returns 404 in production

remediation.note: Catalogue public for GET/HEAD/OPTIONS only; Swagger mounted in production only with API_DOCS_PUBLIC=1; /metrics exemption removed. 5 new tests red before, green after; gateway 115/115. Every app write to products already sends the internal key and the token (Commerce BFF), so nothing that works today is refused. committed locally — pushed when GitHub Actions is back

findings.title: A debug route ships to production
findings.description: src/app/api/debug/route.ts answers GET with whether the caller holds a token, the caller's own tec_user cookie and its verified user id. It reveals nothing about anyone else, but a debug endpoint has no place in production and grows.
findings.root_cause: Left from a debugging session.
findings.technical_impact: Small information surface.
findings.business_impact: None today.

findings.title: A Firebase web API key is in the Hub's service worker
findings.description: tec-frontend/public/firebase-messaging-sw.js holds the Firebase web config key. Firebase web keys are public by design (they identify the project; Firebase rules authorise). It is the only credential-shaped string in the full history of all 30 repositories.
findings.root_cause: By design.
findings.technical_impact: None if the key is restricted.
findings.business_impact: None.

acceptance_criteria: The key shows HTTP-referrer and API restrictions in Google Cloud

findings.title: The instruction files say the session cookies are HttpOnly; ADR-001 says tec_access_token is not
findings.description: Hub and tec-auth CLAUDE.md: 'Hub sets HttpOnly cookies'; ADR-001 (accepted) sets tec_access_token httpOnly:false so Pi Browser can read it, and the code follows the ADR. A reviewer who trusts the instruction file misjudges the risk.
findings.root_cause: Instruction files written before ADR-001.
findings.technical_impact: A wrong mental model of what a script can read.
findings.business_impact: Risk misjudged.
findings.recommendation: State ADR-001 in the instruction files: tec_access_token is readable by script by decision; tec_refresh_token is HttpOnly.
acceptance_criteria: No instruction file says the access token is HttpOnly

remediation.note: Instruction files state ADR-001. committed locally — pushed when GitHub Actions is back

findings.title: A failed load of the wallet history or payment list shows an empty list
findings.description: useWallet.ts:197 and useAppPayments.ts:25 swallow a failed fetch ('transactions are optional'; 'absent beats wrong'). The screen then reads 'no transactions' — a statement about money that is not true — with nothing reported.

evidence.observation: catch { /* the list is optional; absent beats wrong */ }

findings.root_cause: Optional data treated as absent data.
findings.technical_impact: An outage looks like an empty history.
findings.business_impact: A Pioneer may think a payment is missing.
findings.recommendation: Keep the list optional but distinguish 'could not load' from 'none', and reportError the failure.
acceptance_criteria: A failed history request renders an error state and reports it (test)

remediation.note: useWallet sets txError and reports; the page shows "Could not load your transactions" with Retry. wallet-history-failure.test.tsx red before, green after; Hub 177 files green. useAppPayments was already right (null → nothing rendered) — the finding over-counted it. committed locally — pushed when GitHub Actions is back

findings.title: No app but the Hub could renew a session — the refresh token was not kept or not sent
findings.description: sso-callback sets tec_access_token, tec_user and tec_csrf; it never sets tec_refresh_token. /api/auth/refresh sends the refresh cookie if present and otherwise the access token, and pi-auth.ts calls it only after a 401 — when the access token has already expired. So a refresh cannot succeed once it is needed, and the session lasts exactly the access token's lifetime (7 days on Railway). It also means the access token's lifetime cannot be shortened (ADR-001's 24 h) without signing everyone out daily, which would multiply Pi sign-ins — the very load that made Pi Browser stop opening the wallet (10 Nov).
findings.root_cause: The SSO hand-off carries the access token only.
findings.technical_impact: No working refresh path in template apps.
findings.business_impact: Blocks shortening the token lifetime (part of TEC-AUDIT-0018).
findings.recommendation: Hand the refresh token over in the signed SSO payload and set it HttpOnly (C-123 §2 attributes); refresh shortly before expiry, not after a 401. Phone-verify in Pi Browser before shortening JWT_EXPIRES_IN.
acceptance_criteria: A template app holds tec_refresh_token (HttpOnly) after sign-in
With a 10-minute access token, a session survives an hour of use in Pi Browser

remediation.note: Implemented C-123 §4 for every app but the Hub (which already had it): lib/session-refresh.ts + a middleware step renew an expired (or <2 min) access token at the gateway with the HttpOnly, host-only refresh token, once per token, before any BFF call or /api/auth/me; the route runs with the new token and the rotated cookies (with tec_user + tec_csrf) ride the same response; pages never refresh (LAW 2); a failure leaves the request as it came; a rejected token is dropped. sso-callback keeps the app's OWN refresh token (from its pi-login); a Hub hand-off carries none, so no two holders share a single-use token. The refresh route uses the same helper (it sent the access token before — Commerce/Assets sent none in the header, so refresh was broken in all 23 apps). pi-auth no longer logs out on a failed refresh (C-123 §4). Ecommerce's refresh token moved from the shared domain to host-only. Tests: 11 + 4 + 3 shared cases, 3 red on the old code; every app's full suite, tsc and lint green. Committed locally. Phone check in Pi Browser required before shortening JWT_EXPIRES_IN (TEC-AUDIT-0018 part 2). Residual: an Ecommerce refresh cookie set on the shared domain before this fix lives up to 7 days.
remediation.verification: Pi Browser: sign in to an app, wait past a short access-token lifetime, use the app — still signed in

findings.title: The hourly reconciliation completes a paid payment without the payment.completed.v1 event
findings.description: reconcileStalePayments runs every hour (server.ts cron). For a payment Pi shows as paid (developer_completed, or approved + verified) it calls markCompleted, which sets status 'completed' with a bare prisma.payment.update and writes an audit row — but no outbox event. Every consumer that delivers what was bought (commerce subscriptions, asset purchases, identity legend/nexus) listens to payment.completed.v1 only. So a payment the reconciliation rescues is marked paid and delivers nothing. The same gap was closed for the recovery endpoint by completeFromRecovery (conditional updateMany + saveOutboxEvent in one transaction); the cron path was not moved onto it. The update is also not conditional: a live /complete racing the cron can both write 'completed'.

evidence.observation: markCompleted: payment.update to completed + audit log; no saveOutboxEvent
called when Pi shows developer_completed or approved+verified
completeFromRecovery: the conditional, event-emitting path the cron should use

findings.root_cause: Two completion paths: the recovery endpoint was fixed to emit the event; the cron kept its own update.
findings.technical_impact: Invariant #2/#4 hold (Pi verified it, an audit row exists) but the event — the fact consumers act on — is never written (C-47 P4, Forbidden #6 silent failure).
findings.business_impact: A user who paid, whose payment the hourly job finished, gets no Pro / no asset / no order effect. Support sees "completed" and no delivery.
findings.recommendation: markCompleted calls completeFromRecovery (or the same conditional updateMany + saveOutboxEvent in one transaction) and emits only when the row actually transitioned.
acceptance_criteria: A reconciled payment writes exactly one payment.completed.v1 outbox row
A second run, or a racing /complete, writes none
A test fails on the old markCompleted and passes on the new

remediation.note: services/payment-transitions.ts: completeOpenPayment = conditional updateMany (created/approved) + payment.completed.v1 in the same transaction, same envelope as the normal path. The reconciliation uses it; a lost race counts as skipped with no audit row. payment-transitions.test.ts: 4 cases red on the old reconciliation. 469/469, tsc, build. No PR before 1 Dec. Payments the cron completed before the fix still have no event — re-emitting them is a separate, audited, owner-approved step.
remediation.verification: After deploy: a stale approved payment Pi shows as paid → one payment.completed.v1 in outbox_events and the consumer delivers

findings.title: The recovery endpoint can cancel a payment that completed while it was asking Pi
findings.description: resolve-incomplete rejects a payment that is final when it reads it (409), then asks Pi — one or two network round trips — and only then cancels, with an unconditional update. In CASE C the guard at the write is `status !== 'cancelled'` on the status read BEFORE those round trips; the unreachable-on-Pi branch checks all three final states, but also on the old read. A payment completed by a concurrent /complete in that window is rewritten to 'cancelled'. (Corrected on 13 Nov while fixing it: the first text said a locally completed payment passes the guard; the 409 at the top stops that — the gap is the race window.)

evidence.observation: guard at the write is status !== 'cancelled', on a status read before the Pi calls
terminal states checked, then an unconditional update

findings.root_cause: The guard names one terminal state instead of the state machine (ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS).
findings.technical_impact: Terminal → terminal transition: breaks Invariant #7 and Forbidden #9.
findings.business_impact: A paid payment can be shown as cancelled; reports and support disagree with Pi.
findings.recommendation: Both branches use a conditional updateMany with status in ('created','approved') — the transitions ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS permits — and act on the count.
acceptance_criteria: A completed or failed payment is never changed by resolve-incomplete
Test red on the old guard, green on the new

remediation.note: Both cancel branches of resolve-incomplete use cancelOpenPayment (conditional on created/approved in the WHERE); the audit is written only when the row changed. Controller test for the race: red on the old code.
remediation.verification: Covered by the unit test; no runtime step needed

findings.title: approve and complete read the payment, then update it by id — a check-then-act
findings.description: Both run inside a transaction but update with where: { id } after a separate read of the status, so two concurrent calls can both pass the check. The effect is limited: complete may write two outbox events, and every consumer is idempotent by paymentId (asset upsert by paymentId; subscription returns early on the same payment_id).
findings.root_cause: Read and write are separate statements without a status condition.
findings.technical_impact: Possible duplicate payment.completed.v1; absorbed by idempotent consumers.
findings.business_impact: None observed.
findings.recommendation: Conditional updateMany on the expected from-state, as completeFromRecovery does; emit only on count 1.
acceptance_criteria: Two concurrent completes produce one event

remediation.note: approve and complete use the controller's transitionPayment: the from-state is in the WHERE; count 0 → the loser writes nothing, queues nothing, answers 409 INVALID_STATUS (what a sequential duplicate already got). Three cases in terminal-state-race.test.ts, red on the old code. 472/472, tsc, build.
remediation.verification: Covered by the unit tests

findings.title: 437 of 465 gateway calls from the apps' BFF routes have no timeout
findings.description: BFF routes call `${GATEWAY}/api/...` with fetch and no AbortSignal. The gateway itself now bounds slow upstreams (NEW-W), but when the gateway is the slow part — the 'Backend Offline' freeze — every pending BFF call waits until Vercel kills the function, and the screen shows a spinner instead of the state screen. The template's own session-refresh (8 s) is one of the 28 that do set one.

evidence.observation: 439/467 calls, every app 1–4 with a signal
gateway-side timeouts exist; app-side do not

findings.root_cause: No shared gateway-fetch helper; each route calls fetch directly.
findings.technical_impact: A slow gateway ties up a function per pending call; failures surface late and as timeouts, not as the 502/504 the screens handle.
findings.business_impact: During an incident users see endless loading instead of "try again".
findings.recommendation: One shared gatewayFetch(path, init) in the template (AbortSignal.timeout, default 10 s) used by every BFF route; template-sync carries it.
acceptance_criteria: No BFF fetch to the gateway without a timeout (a check in CI)
A test: a hung gateway → the route answers 504 within the limit

refs: the guard in every other app
remediation.note: src/lib/gateway-fetch.ts (shared via template-sync): fetch with a deadline just past the gateway's own 504 (25 s) — 30 s, 90 s for an /ai/ path (the gateway waits 75 s for TEC AI) — so a live gateway always answers first and nothing it would complete is cut (a payment approve included); a caller's own signal still works. 435 gateway calls in 25 repositories (437 matched, the Hub's 2 own-origin calls then restored) moved onto it by a codemod; gateway-fetch.test.ts (shared) checks the deadlines and fails on any bare gateway fetch left in src/, with a self-check that the search finds one. Each repository: tsc, lint and its full suite green. Correction: two of the 467 calls counted in Run 3 were the Hub calling its OWN origin (${req.nextUrl.origin}/api/auth/refresh) — not gateway calls; they are left as they were and the search now exempts own-origin calls. True count: 465 gateway calls, 437 without a deadline. | Second pass (14 Nov 2026), found while bringing Life onto the template: the first sweep and its guard matched only fetch(`${X}/api/`, so every call whose URL is built first passed — `${GW}${path}` in the one helper each of seven apps routes its whole BFF through (Life, Zone, Nexus, Explorer, System, Connection, Analytics), fetch(url, …) in the shared GET helper of Commerce, Assets and Ecommerce and in Commerce payouts, fetch(BASE|url|target, …) in ten Hub routes (admin erasure, void-balances, account-merge, life-ai ×2, seller-liabilities, reconcile, assets, notifications mark-read), Explorer reviews. All now go through gatewayFetch. Non-gateway server calls with none got their own deadline: seven uploads to object storage (60 s), the OKX price (8 s), the Hub's AI-provider probes (30 s), Upstash rate-limit (2 s, falls back to memory as on any error), fetchWithRetry (30 s per attempt). The guard now judges EVERY fetch( in server code by its arguments (signal required unless the URL is relative or the app's own origin); its self-check holds seven bare shapes and five exempt ones; red on the old code and green after in each of the six apps changed in the second step (git stash). Lesson recorded: the first guard was checked to FIND a call, but only in the shape the sweep had already fixed — a self-check proves the search finds what it was written for, not what it was not. Note: the Hub's admin reconcile calls payment-service directly (PAYMENT_SERVICE_URL), not through the gateway — it has a deadline now; whether that call should exist is for P5 of the next cycle.
remediation.verification: After deploy, with the gateway stopped: a BFF route answers with its error within ~30 s instead of hanging

findings.title: The BFFs bypass the server SDK: one file per app imports it, and gateway responses are not schema-validated
findings.description: C-47 §14 says public integration goes through @yasser172/tec-sdk and every response is Zod-validated. In practice each app imports the SDK in a single file (src/lib/sdk.ts; none at all in Assets, Commerce, Life) and makes its 400+ gateway calls with raw fetch, reading the JSON as-is. The SDK itself was last changed on 13 Sep (1.4.0). So the contract the SDK is meant to pin is not the contract the apps use, and a backend shape change reaches the screens unchecked — the class of the nested-envelope Pro-status bug the template already documents.
findings.root_cause: The SDK covers payment/auth; domain routes were written straight against the gateway.
findings.technical_impact: Forbidden #5 (divergent SDK contract vs backend) cannot be detected; responses are trusted unvalidated.
findings.business_impact: A backend change can silently blank a screen or mis-gate a paid feature in many apps at once.
findings.recommendation: Do not wrap 400 calls at once. Decide in an ADR whether domain calls belong in the SDK; meanwhile validate at the edge with the shared gatewayFetch (0033) taking a zod schema for the money and entitlement routes first.
acceptance_criteria: An ADR records where domain contracts live
Payment, wallet and subscription BFF responses are schema-checked

remediation.note: Scheduled after Run 3. Seen during 0007: the Hub's BFF PATCH /api/bff/identity/profile sends `avatar`; identity's route reads `avatarUrl` — the avatar sent that way is never saved. One more contract the SDK would pin.

findings.title: The template's example route /api/bff/items calls a gateway path that does not exist
findings.description: Of 712 gateway paths the apps call, 709 match a route in the gateway registry. The other three: two are tests that call the app's own origin, and the third is /api/items, called by the example route src/app/api/bff/items that the template ships and 20 apps still carry. No gateway prefix serves it, so the live route can only fail.
findings.root_cause: A copy-me example kept in production builds.
findings.technical_impact: A public route that always errors; noise in logs and error reports.
findings.business_impact: None to users unless something links to it.
findings.recommendation: Move the example out of src/app (e.g. docs/examples) in the template; remove it from the apps that do not use it.
acceptance_criteria: No app ships /api/bff/items unless the gateway serves /api/items

refs: the copy in 18 apps (one commit each, 14 Nov)
remediation.note: The example moved to docs/examples/bff-route.example.ts (still type-checked); removed from the 20 apps where it was the unchanged copy and nothing called it; template-sync carries the example and the helper instead. | 14 Nov: the copy itself, listed as shared but never carried into the apps, added to the 18 template apps (type-checked in each); template-sync check: every one matches (NBF's recorded exception aside). Life and Zone get it with 0005.
remediation.verification: No app builds a /api/bff/items route

findings.title: Notifications, live updates and analytics miss every payment completed off the normal path
findings.description: A completed payment is announced on two streams. payment.completed.v1 is durable (outbox, same transaction). The unversioned payment.completed is a direct publish after the response: skipped when the Redis publisher is not ready (the log says the outbox will retry — not for this stream), and never sent by the recovery endpoint or the hourly reconciliation. Wallet and commerce moved to .v1; notification, realtime and analytics still read only the unversioned stream. The catalog still lists wallet and commerce as its consumers; the drift check compares names, not consumers.
findings.root_cause: A migration to the versioned stream (audit F-2, Aug) moved the money consumers and stopped there.
findings.technical_impact: Three consumers see a subset of completions; the subset depends on Redis readiness and on which path completed the payment.
findings.business_impact: A paying user may get no "payment received" notification and no live update; analytics under-counts revenue.
findings.recommendation: Move the three consumers to payment.completed.v1 (each idempotent by paymentId), then remove both direct publishes; fix the catalog; make check-drift compare consumer groups.
acceptance_criteria: A completion through recovery produces a notification
No code publishes the unversioned payment.completed
check-drift fails on a stale consumer list

remediation.note: notification, realtime and analytics dual-read both streams, once per paymentId; the payment log is truthful; check-drift compares consumers (found 4 stale entries) and the catalog is corrected. Retiring the legacy publish is a later change, after the consumers are deployed.
remediation.verification: After deploy: a payment finished by resolve-incomplete produces a notification and a live update

findings.repository: tec-template-base + 19 apps (all but Life of those that declare it)
findings.title: The 60 % coverage floor is declared in 21 app repositories and enforced in one
findings.description: Each vitest.config declares thresholds (60/60/60/50); CI runs npm test without coverage and @vitest/coverage-v8 is not installed, so the floor never runs. Only Tec-Life runs test:coverage. The Hub, Assets, Commerce and Ecommerce declare no floor at all. Measured here, the template is at 69.5/61.2/63.9/74.9.

evidence.observation: floor declared; CI runs npm test

findings.root_cause: The floor was added to the config; the CI step and dependency were not.
findings.technical_impact: Coverage can fall to zero without CI noticing.
findings.business_impact: A gate everyone believes in that never runs.
findings.recommendation: Template: add @vitest/coverage-v8 and run test:coverage in CI; carry it by template-sync; measure each app first and set its floor no higher than it passes.
acceptance_criteria: CI fails when coverage falls below the floor in every app

remediation.note: CI runs test:coverage in every app (Life already did); the Hub could not measure at all (duplicate provider) — fixed; four apps below the fleet floor hold a ratchet at their measured level. Open: the template apps measure only the files their tests load — moving to every file in src/ needs the same ratchet, app by app.
remediation.verification: CI fails when coverage falls below the floor in every app

findings.title: No test crosses a service boundary — event contracts are checked by neither side
findings.description: Each event's producer and consumers test against their own hand-written payloads; nothing checks that the stream name and shape one side writes is what the other reads. This cycle's costliest defects lived exactly there: commerce's order consumer was never registered and listened on the wrong stream (its own comment), the reconciliation wrote no event (0030), three consumers read a best-effort stream (0036). The two tests that use a real database skip in CI although the job already runs a Postgres.

evidence.observation: skip without TEST_DATABASE_URL; CI has Postgres

findings.root_cause: Tests are per service; the stream is nobody's test.
findings.technical_impact: A renamed stream or field passes every suite and fails silently in production.
findings.business_impact: Purchases not delivered, with green CI.
findings.recommendation: A contract fixture per event under shared/: the producer test asserts its real payload equals the fixture; each consumer test feeds the fixture through its handler. Set TEST_DATABASE_URL to the CI Postgres for the two real-database tests.
acceptance_criteria: Changing a field in the outbox payload fails a consumer test
The two real-database tests run in CI

remediation.note: shared/contracts/payment.completed.v1.json; one payload builder in payment-service, checked against it; commerce (subscription + order) and asset feed its examples through their real handlers; CI re-runs them on a contract change; the two real-database tests run on the job's Postgres. Not yet under contract: trust (legend), nexus, wallet.
remediation.verification: Changing a field in the contract fails CI in the producer and the consumers

findings.title: Deploy-safety settings for 19 of 20 services exist only in Railway's dashboard
findings.description: Only tec-api-gateway keeps its Railway settings in the repo (railway.toml: healthcheckPath, healthcheckTimeout, stopTimeoutSeconds). For the other 19 the Healthcheck Path, the start command and 'Wait for CI' live in the dashboard only. The migrate-on-start script refuses to start on any doubt and depends on a healthcheck to keep the old deployment live; without one the service goes DOWN (payment-service, most of 8 Nov). Nothing in code says which services have it. Owner, 13 Nov: 'Wait for CI' is off on every service — a merge deploys immediately, with no CI behind it while Actions is refused.

evidence.observation: the only Railway config in the repo
"The service MUST have a Healthcheck Path" — set by hand

findings.root_cause: Railway was configured service by service in the UI.
findings.technical_impact: A service created or edited without the healthcheck turns a refused migration into an outage; nobody can review it.
findings.business_impact: Repeat of 8 Nov: payments down for hours.
findings.recommendation: A railway.toml per service (config-as-code): healthcheckPath '/health', healthcheckTimeout, startCommand 'npm start', stopTimeoutSeconds; a CI check that every service has one with a health path.
acceptance_criteria: Every service directory has railway.toml with healthcheckPath
CI fails on a service without it

remediation.note: railway.toml with healthcheckPath "/health" in all 19 services; CI policy check. Owner: confirm Railway reads it from the service root.
remediation.verification: A deploy whose migrate step refuses keeps the old deployment live

findings.title: Every scheduled safety check runs on GitHub Actions — all stopped since 12 Nov; the restore check passes when unconfigured
findings.description: 31 scheduled jobs — weekly CodeQL in 28 repositories, the KB's weekly drift check, the template's weekly fleet-drift, the monthly backup restore check — all on GitHub Actions, refused for the account since 12 Nov. None has run since; the next restore check is due 3 Dec. Separately, restore-check.yml passes with a notice when its secrets are missing, so a renamed secret would make it green and silent (it was configured and proven 12 Oct and 10 Nov). Owner, 13 Nov: ALERT_WEBHOOK_URL is not set on backup-job, so a failed nightly backup only marks the Railway cron run failed and alerts nobody — with the restore check stopped as well, a broken backup goes unseen.

evidence.observation: the check was real when configured

findings.root_cause: One provider for every guard; a check written to skip rather than fail.
findings.technical_impact: Security scans, drift and restore verification stop together with one billing problem.
findings.business_impact: A broken backup could go unnoticed until it is needed.
findings.recommendation: Set ALERT_WEBHOOK_URL on backup-job (owner; e.g. a free Discord channel webhook). Fail the restore check when unconfigured (exit 1). Run the restore check also as a Railway cron next to the backup (the code is already in tec-backup-job), so it does not depend on GitHub billing; record which guards run where in C-78.
acceptance_criteria: The restore check fails red when its secrets are missing
A restore check runs monthly without GitHub Actions

remediation.note: Restore check fails when unconfigured; RESTORE_LOCAL_POSTGRES=1 lets it run as a Railway cron (end-to-end tested). Owner: create the cron service (README step 5); ALERT_WEBHOOK_URL deferred (risk accepted).
remediation.verification: The Railway cron restore check runs green on 3 Dec

findings.title: Public directory searches return every match, uncapped, through a full-table substring scan
findings.description: Explorer search (explorer.service.ts:235) and NX search (nx.service.ts:112) are public routes that return every matching row with no take and no page. Explorer matches each word with `contains` on search_text, whose btree index cannot serve LIKE '%…%'. An empty query returns the whole directory.
findings.root_cause: Written for a small directory.
findings.technical_impact: Response size and database time grow linearly with the directory; one request can read the whole table.
findings.business_impact: Slow discovery as merchants join; an easy load amplifier.
findings.recommendation: A take (e.g. 50) with a cursor on both; for Explorer a pg_trgm GIN index on search_text (a migration) or Postgres full-text search.
acceptance_criteria: Both searches answer at most one page
EXPLAIN shows an index scan for a word query

remediation.note: Both searches paged (≤100, hasMore); pg_trgm GIN index on search_text (migration).
remediation.verification: EXPLAIN on production uses the trigram index

findings.title: No app pins the Node version it builds on
findings.description: No engines.node and no .nvmrc in any of 25 app repositories; CI uses Node 22, Vercel uses each project's dashboard setting. A change on Vercel's side builds production on a version CI never ran.
findings.root_cause: Never declared.
findings.technical_impact: Build/runtime drift between CI and production.
findings.business_impact: A surprise build break or behaviour change on deploy.
findings.recommendation: "engines": { "node": "22.x" } in the template (template-sync dependency pin) and every app.
acceptance_criteria: Every app declares engines.node

remediation.note: engines.node 22.x everywhere; template-sync marker. | 14 Nov: fc5a570 (this finding's template fix) broke template-sync.test — it added a marker on package.json ("node": "22.x") and the test rewrote package.json compactly, erasing it. The template's full suite had not been run on that commit; found when it was. Fixed in the test (it writes the file the way it is written).
remediation.verification: Vercel build logs show Node 22

findings.title: Capacity has never been measured, and no latency objective exists
findings.description: k6 scripts exist (gateway, payment; workflow_dispatch only) but no run is recorded anywhere in the KB; slo-definitions.yaml sets availability targets only. How many users the platform carries is unknown.
findings.root_cause: No staging to run them against (0006).
findings.technical_impact: Limits are discovered in production, as in June.
findings.business_impact: Launch capacity is a guess.
findings.recommendation: p95 latency objectives for gateway, auth and payment in slo-definitions.yaml; one recorded k6 run against a preview/staging once 0006 gives one.
acceptance_criteria: A recorded k6 run in runtime-evidence/
Latency SLOs defined

remediation.note: Latency SLOs defined (C-78 §2, slo-definitions.yaml). A recorded k6 run waits on staging (0006).
remediation.verification: A recorded k6 run in runtime-evidence/

findings.title: Eleven files are copied into 8–18 apps with no tracker, and some have already diverged
findings.description: Source files identical in 8–18 apps and in none of template-sync's lists (shared, fleet, markers): bff/subscription, auth/me, the Pro cancel button, ErrorBoundary, i18n, useMe, and the referral loop (route, RefApply, RefCapture, InviteCard, lib-client/referral). Among 7 sampled apps auth/me — the session check — exists in 3 versions and the cancel button in 4. The referral loop (C-133) is in 16 apps but not in the template, so a new app is born without it. A fix to any of them reaches one app, and fleet-drift does not notice.
findings.root_cause: Features rolled out by copying, before template-sync existed, and never registered after.
findings.technical_impact: Silent divergence of session and entitlement logic across the fleet.
findings.business_impact: A sign-in or Pro bug fixed in one app stays in the others.
findings.recommendation: Put the referral loop in the template; reconcile each of the 11 to one version (diff, pick, test); add them to shared (or markers where an app must customise).
acceptance_criteria: Every file present in ≥5 apps is in a template-sync list
auth/me is one version fleet-wide

remediation.note: Run 6 remediation. | 14 Nov. Measured first, per file across the 20 template apps, then by behaviour (comments and whitespace set aside): auth/me had two behaviours (17 plain, 3 that log WHICH session cookies a refused request carried — names only; how C-123 §11 was found) → the diagnostic one, with its helper and test; useMe identical in behaviour in all 20 → one; ErrorBoundary and CancelProButton → the template's (tokens; the button reads both subscription shapes — the apps' copy read only one); the referral loop (C-133), in 16 apps and not in the template → into the template, wired in its layout, with the first test it has had anywhere; payment/create identical in behaviour in 19 of 20 (NBF/Brookfield differ in layout only) → the template's, which imports APP_SOURCE instead of declaring it a second time; sso-callback-carry-on (the template's version also checks the handoff-entry fix the apps already had), pi-network (with System's ADR-007 guards — the Pi SDK never loads in a Hub-owned session; passes in all 20). An app's own version stays as a recorded exception with its reason (its translated copy or palette; no referral loop in Analytics/Explorer/NBF/Brookfield — the owner's product decision). All 20: template-sync matches; type-check, lint and every test green (Analytics' auth test faked a request with only cookies.get — completed). Correction to the acceptance criterion: 'every file in ≥5 apps' is wrong — 13 of the 20 such paths are each app's own by nature (icon, page, privacy, app-meta, texts). The right criterion is every file that SHOULD be identical, and those are listed. Left, by design question rather than copying: the subscription route (two contracts: the template's flat ProState vs the apps' commerce envelope; Alert's SettingsView would read Pro as Free on the flat one) — tracked now by a marker on its Testnet rule; unifying it means every app's Pro card reading lib/subscription/pro-status.ts, which no app has yet; i18n/index (5 versions), tec-design-tokens.css (7), app.test (8) — per-app theme and language. | 14 Nov, later — the subscription contract, done by expand–contract (expand only): lib/subscription/read-pro-state.ts, a pure reader for commerce's envelope AND the apps' flat route, fail-closed (paid plan + isActive exactly true + not expired + period not ended); the server resolver and every screen use it. Its tests pin the six shapes commerce's app-subscription.service really returns; pro-reader-guard.test.ts fails any screen that reads /api/bff/subscription by hand (red in every app before). Measured first: the hand readers had TWO rules — SettingsView (19 apps) ignored expiry, the Pro card counted a missing isActive as active — that agreed only because commerce sends plan FREE for every non-entitled state. Found and fixed on the way: (1) Analytics' and Connection's settings read d.subscription without unwrapping `data` — a paying user's settings said FREE; (2) Life's home page fell back to the HUB plan in the tec_user cookie while loading or on a failed read — another app's entitlement and a client-side claim (owner's per-app decision 2026-10-02; P6); now pinned by a test, red on the old page; (3) the template resolver counted a paid plan as active without isActive (commerce never sends that; now it would not pass). The CONTRACT half (routes all answering the flat shape) is left: with every reader tolerant of both shapes, it is now a change to one route per app, not to forty screens. | Contract half done the same day: /api/bff/subscription, lib/subscription/pro-status.ts and app-pro.test.ts are shared — every template app's route answers the resolver's flat ProState (System excepted: it sells no Pro). Visible difference: none — with no session the route now answers FREE (200) where it answered 401, and every screen ended at FREE either way. Remaining under this finding: i18n/index (5 versions), tec-design-tokens.css (7), app.test (8) — each app's own language and theme, kept per app by design.
remediation.verification: fleet-drift on main lists no app; the subscription contract has its own item

findings.title: The fleet does not run the same TEC packages — and the Hub runs none of the UI or auth ones
findings.description: tec-ui 3.0.0 in 21 apps, 2.1.0 (the pre-amber palette, C-83) in Assets, Commerce and Ecommerce. tec-sdk 1.4.0 is published and used by no app (21 on 1.3.0, 4 on 1.2.2). The Hub depends on neither tec-ui nor tec-auth, although its CLAUDE.md lists both and says a tec-ui bump must deploy all four apps together.
findings.root_cause: Releases without a fleet bump; the Hub grew its own implementations.
findings.technical_impact: Two visual palettes and three SDK contracts live at once; the shared auth package does not cover the identity authority itself.
findings.business_impact: Inconsistent look between apps; an SDK fix reaches nobody until each app bumps.
findings.recommendation: Bump Assets/Commerce/Ecommerce to tec-ui ^3 (C-83); every app to the current tec-sdk after 0019; decide by ADR whether the Hub adopts tec-auth/tec-ui or the instructions say it does not.
acceptance_criteria: One tec-ui major and one tec-sdk minor fleet-wide
The Hub instructions match its dependencies

remediation.note: Run 6 remediation. | 14 Nov. tec-ui: Assets/Commerce/Ecommerce pinned EXACTLY 2.1.0 (so 3.x never arrived) → ^3.0.0 (C-83; no export changed). tec-sdk: every range was ^1.2.2, the lockfiles differed (21 on 1.3.0, the Hub and the older three on 1.2.2) → ^1.4.0 everywhere but the Hub (1.3.1 packaging, 1.4.0 adds an analytics client — additive). Moving Ecommerce to 1.4.0 failed its production build: browser code reached the server SDK — lib-client/pi/pi-auth.ts → lib/sdk.ts → @yasser172/tec-sdk, which since 1.3.0 imports node's async_hooks. A new test (sdk-boundary.test.ts, shared; follows imports transitively from every 'use client' file and src/lib-client) found the same path in the template and 21 of 25 repos — latent where no page imports pi-auth, live in Ecommerce and the Hub. Its two uses could not work in a browser (clearAuthToken held nothing; resolveIncomplete had no gateway address — the Hub's SDK falls back to http://localhost:4000). Fixed in the template, the 20 apps, Ecommerce and the Hub: resolvePendingPayment goes through the app's own resolve-incomplete route; the browser 'SDK step' is gone. Red before and green after; production builds pass (template, Commerce, Assets, Ecommerce, Hub). The Hub instructions now say what it depends on (no tec-ui, no tec-auth, no packages/ folder). LEFT (owner decision): the Hub's lib-client/pi/pi-payment.ts → lib/sdk.ts for getPaymentStatus() — no production caller, cannot work in a browser; remove it, or a server route that checks the caller owns the payment. Until then the Hub stays on tec-sdk 1.2.2 and its boundary test names that one path. Also the owner's: whether the Hub adopts tec-ui / tec-auth (ADR). | 14 Nov, later (owner: 'كمل' on the recommendation): getPaymentStatus() removed from the Hub's lib-client/pi/pi-payment.ts and PiRuntime with the six tests that exercised it against a mocked SDK; the Hub's boundary test now names no exception (red with the old file, green after); the Hub moves to tec-sdk ^1.4.0 — type-check, lint, 3,267 tests and a production build pass. Both acceptance criteria hold locally: one tec-ui major (^3, every app that uses it) and one tec-sdk minor (^1.4.0, all 25 repos); the Hub's instructions match its dependencies. Whether the Hub ADOPTS tec-ui/tec-auth stays an open design decision (ADR), not part of this finding.
remediation.verification: On main: every repo's lockfile resolves tec-sdk 1.4.x and (where used) tec-ui 3.x; sdk-boundary.test.ts green in every app
